segments.text: Army studies of artillery fire uncovered a brutal piece of battlefield clockwork.
When shells start falling on soldiers caught in the open, roughly two-thirds of all casualties
happen in the first five to ten seconds.
After ten seconds, everyone who is still alive is flat in a trench or behind cover, and ten
minutes of steady shelling after that achieves only a fraction of what the opening burst
did.
A conventional howitzer can only put one shell into that first ten-second window.
In 1941, Soviet engineers answered that arithmetic by bolting steel rails to the back of ordinary
trucks.
A single battery of Katusha launchers could throw more than four tons of high explosive onto
a target in under ten seconds, turning a square kilometer of forest into splinters before
the soldiers underneath could throw themselves into the dirt.
That ten-second window sets up the question this video answers.
Compared to a normal artillery gun, a rocket is expensive, bulky to haul, and leaves a smoke
trail across the sky that points straight back to the launcher.
Why does every modern army still rely on rocket artillery alongside tube guns, and how did
a weapon famous for spraying whole grid squares turn into a long-range sniper?
The answer follows the parts of the system itself, because each piece of a modern rocket launcher
exists to keep the shock of that ten-second salvo while curing the flaws that came with it.
Start with the mechanical difference that makes the salvo possible.
When a conventional howitzer fires, all the propellant burns inside a sealed steel chamber at once, driving
the shell down the barrel under immense pressure.
Containing that explosion takes a barrel weighing several tons and a heavy hydraulic recoil mechanism
to keep the gun from tearing itself off its carriage.
That weight is why a self-propelled gun carries only one barrel.
A rocket flips that engineering inside-out.
Instead of leaving the propellant in the gun, the rocket carries its solid fuel motor inside
its own body and vents the hot gas straight out the back through a nozzle.
Because the exhaust shoots freely out the rear of an open tube, there is almost no recoil
pushing against the vehicle.
The launch tube does not need to be a forged steel pressure vessel.
Mechanically, the tubes on a launcher like the Soviet BM-21 Grad are little more than thin-walled
guide pipes, whose only job is to hold the rocket pointed at the right angle for the first half-second
of its flight.
Freed from the weight of a heavy barrel and breech, an ordinary six-wheeled truck can carry
forty-one hundred twenty-two-millimeter tubes on its back and ripple-fire the entire load
in twenty seconds.
The truck only needs hydraulic jacks to keep the suspension from rocking between shots,
and steel shutters that fold over the windshield so the roaring flame from the nozzles does
not shatter the cab glass over the crew's heads.
Trading a heavy barrel for open tubes comes with a fierce penalty in accuracy.
A howitzer shell finishes burning its powder before it leaves the muzzle, so it exits the
barrel at top speed and spinning fast.
A rocket crawls out of its tube relatively slowly and keeps burning fuel for several seconds while
climbing through the sky.
If a crosswind pushes against the tail fins while the motor is still thrusting, the tail
gets blown sideways and tilts the nose into the wind, so the rocket actually steers itself
off course while accelerating.
Add the fact that the rocket gets lighter every millisecond as its fuel burns away, and even
a tiny difference in propellant temperature changes where it lands.
To tame that wobble without guidance computers, designers cut shallow spiral grooves inside
the launch tube to give the rocket an initial spin and fit spring-loaded fins that snap open
the instant the tail clears the tube.
For decades, that was only enough to keep a salvo inside a broad oval hundreds of meters
wide.
Rocket systems from the 40 tube grad up to the giant 300 millimeter smirch were built
as area weapons.
Their warheads were packed with pre-scored fragmentation rings, scatterable anti-tank mines, sub-munitions,
or fuel air explosives designed to blanket an entire assembly area, an airfield, or a supply
depot in one sudden storm.
Blanketing an area creates two new headaches right away.
First, 40 rockets flying out of one truck leave a giant curtain of white exhaust smoke and
scorched grass that every drone and spotter for 20 kiminers can see immediately.
Second, once a classical launcher like the Grad empties its tubes, soldiers have to stand
in the open and slide 40 heavy rockets back into the pipes by hand, one after another, which
can take 20 or 30 minutes of exhausting labor right when enemy counter battery fire is on
the way.
Western designers solved that reload trap in the late cold war with the tracked M270 multiple
launch rocket system and its lighter wheeled cousin, the M142 HIMARS.
Instead of mounting permanent tubes that have to be stuffed by hand, these launchers carry
sealed rectangular pods made of aluminum and fiberglass.
Each pod holds six 227-millimeter rockets, packed and wired at the factory, so the pod itself serves
as both the shipping crate and the launch tubes.
Built right into the launcher's frame is a mechanical crane and winch.
After firing, the vehicle drives to a hidden roadside spot where a supply truck has dropped
a fresh pod on the ground, winches the empty box off, hooks up the full one in about five minutes
without a crewman ever touching a bare rocket, and drives off again.
The pod solved reloading, and then electronics turned the rocket's old accuracy problem on its head.
Because a rocket is much wider than an artillery shell and accelerates gently rather than being
hammered by a single violent explosion in a gun breach, it is far easier to pack delicate
electronics into its nose. Engineers fitted the 227-millimeter rocket with an inertial guidance
unit paired with a satellite navigation receiver and four small steering canards at the tip.
The result, known as the guided multiple launch rocket, changed the role of the entire weapon.
Instead of firing 12 unguided rockets to be sure of hitting one target 40 Commodores away,
a single guided rocket from a high Mars pod can launch one guided rocket over 70 Commodores
and drop a 90-kilogram warhead within a few meters of a specific bridge pier, radar van, or ammunition
bunker. If the target is even farther back, that exact same six rocket pod can be swapped for an
identical-looking pod holding a single massive tactical ballistic missile, such as a TACIMS,
which reaches out to 300 Commodores. There is a quiet irony in that evolution.
A weapon family that was invented only because rockets were too clumsy to hit a single building,
ended up becoming the tool armies used to hit a specific room from 80 Commodores away.
Even so, rocket artillery has a logistics appetite that terrifies quartermasters.
A single six rocket pod weighs well over two tons. A launcher that fires two pods in 10 minutes has
just thrown four tons of precision hardware downrange, and there is no cheap way to manufacture rocket
motors and guidance fins at the speed they can be launched. A rocket crew can comfortably spend a
brigade's weekly ammunition budget in the time it takes to boil a kettle and then spend the rest of
the day hiding under trees waiting for a supply truck. Which brings us to the common mistake people
make when they watch guided rockets in the news. Viewers see precision strikes blowing up distant
depots and wonder why armies bother keeping old-fashioned tube howitzers at all. My own reading is
that tube artillery and rocket artillery are not competitors doing the same job at different prices.
Tube artillery is the steady heartbeat of the front line, firing relatively cheap shells all afternoon to
pin trenches and break up assaults five or ten commiliters away. Rocket artillery is the long-handled
sledgehammer kept in reserve behind the line, brought out for two minutes to smash a command post,
a river crossing, or a massed column 50 commiliters deep, shaping the battle before the infantry ever
meets it. So return to those first 10 seconds of an artillery strike, when soldiers caught above ground
have not yet dived for cover. Everything in a modern rocket launcher, the recoilless open tubes,
the folding tail fins, the crane-loaded pod, and the satellite-steered nosecone,
traces back to the katusha trucks of 1941. A howitzer fights a battle over hours. Rocket artillery exists
to compress an entire afternoon of destruction into the few seconds before the enemy can blink.
